note: Closing IDEAS §6.40 — the human surface could be aimed at a custom domain and could not be told the matcher that keys it. The entry deliberately declined to propose a fix, naming two candidates and saying the choice wanted an adversarial read first. These are the decisions that read produced. Then an audit found three defects in the fix itself, two of them the same category error one level up; the last three decisions are what that audit forced.

decisions.question: Between §6.40's two candidate fixes — give the surface a matcher, or stop it recomputing a key it was already holding — which is right?
decisions.commitment: The matcher field. The smaller fix repairs one path and cannot answer for the others.
decisions.why: 'Reuse the stored key' works only where a stored key exists, and that is exactly one endpoint: seal-draft, which loads a row and has its source_norm in hand. It has nothing to say for /api/seal, which takes raw text and no row; for /api/reject-match, which keys a *query* that was never stored and never will be; or for /api/ask and /api/match, which must key something to score anything. Each of those must normalize, and in a custom domain the only correct normalizer is the domain's. The smaller fix would also make the surface structurally unable to re-key a row whose matcher changed, which is a repair a curator will eventually want and which reusing a stale key forecloses. The entry was right to hesitate and right that this needed arguing rather than patching; the argument just comes out one way.

decisions.question: What does `App.matcher = None` mean — StringMatcher, or defer?
decisions.commitment: Defer to the process-wide matcher. `--matcher string` resolves to None rather than constructing a StringMatcher.
decisions.why: A host that called memory.set_matcher() before launching the surface has already said what keys its domain. Building a StringMatcher for the default flag value would silently override that, which is the same class of act as the defect being fixed: substituting a matcher behind a caller's back. The distinction costs one conditional and is the difference between a default that means 'nothing specified' and one that means 'I have decided it is StringMatcher'. Only the first is true of a flag the caller did not pass.

decisions.question: When a request names a matcher on a domain that has its own, which wins?
decisions.commitment: A name that AGREES with the domain's matcher is honoured; a name that disagrees is a 400. Never a silent substitution.
decisions.why: Both silent answers are wrong. Honouring a different name scores the query under a different notion of similarity than the one that sealed the rows, which produces a confident wrong answer to the only question this product is ever asked. Ignoring the name and using the domain's returns a result the caller will read as an answer about the matcher they asked for. So a genuine disagreement is refused, the same reasoning build_matcher already applies to an unknown name. The first version refused ANY name, which was right in principle and wrong in practice — see the separate decision on what that cost the browser; a caller asking for what is already in force is not asking for something else, and treating those two as one is what broke the Match view.

decisions.question: Does §6.41's optional `score()` become mandatory, now that its question is live?
decisions.commitment: No. Stopping the re-keying answers it, and promoting the method would break every matcher written against the documented two.
decisions.why: §6.41 measured that a matcher implementing the optional score() never consults the key at all, so it survived this defect while one implementing exactly the documented seam lost a human's verification. That made an optional method load-bearing for a correctness guarantee, which is untenable — but the fix is to remove the load, not to make the method compulsory. Mandating it would punish every author who implemented what the README asked, to compensate for a bug in the caller. What is worth keeping from §6.41 is not the design question, which is now closed, but the epistemics: a defect that spares whoever did MORE than the documentation asked, and bites whoever did exactly what it asked, is invisible to the person who wrote the documentation, because they are the most likely to have done more.

decisions.question: The fixture that measured the gap asserts the gap still exists. What happens to it?
decisions.commitment: Every beat kept, every outcome inverted. Eight gap() assertions become claim()s, plus a new test asserting the old sentences never come back.
decisions.why: demo/two_desks.py was built with a gap() helper that fails the build when a gap *closes*, on the reasoning that a demo narrating a gap somebody fixed is the same defect as one narrating a fix that never landed. That mechanism did its job here: shipping the fix without rewriting the narrative would have stopped the build. Deleting the fixture instead would have thrown away the only executable statement of what the defect was — so it is kept, asking the same questions, and a regression puts the old answers back where a test now looks for them. The narrative also had to stop being written in the present tense about a broken thing, which is a larger edit than it sounds and the reason the diff is mostly prose.

decisions.question: How is a fix like this shown to work, when the defect produced a 200 and a valid signature?
decisions.commitment: Mutation after the fix, not only before — and record which tests do NOT fail under it.
decisions.why: The whole character of this defect is that it looks like success from every surface a caller can reach, so a test that checks the endpoint returns 200, or that a sealed row exists, would have passed throughout. Reverting the seven threading call sites turns 8 of 12 red; the 4 that stay green are the ones about the App field and the 400 refusal rather than the threading. Recording that split matters more than the count: a test that passes under the mutation it was written to catch proves nothing, and knowing which of yours are in that category is the difference between a suite and a decoration. §6.40's own history makes the point — its first beat-7 assertion was vacuous, comparing keys that were byte-identical for the string chosen.

decisions.question: Does App.matcher apply to every request the surface handles?
decisions.commitment: No. Only to the domain it describes. Every other domain defers to the process-wide default.
decisions.why: The first version passed app.matcher to every keying call, and an audit caught what that costs: /api/reject-match is shared by every recipe, so the Entity view — which rejects an alias carrying the *entity* domain, keyed by EntityResolver's own StringMatcher — began filing rejections under the incident domain's matcher. HTTP 200, a real signature, a rejection nothing looks up, and the wrong entity served again. That is §6.40's exact symptom, produced by §6.40's fix, one recipe over. The rule that falls out is sharper than the original fix: a matcher keys ONE domain, so an App holding the tags of one and the matcher of the same one must not lend that matcher to a request about another. It also settles the per-request-tags question the audit raised separately — the Ask and Match views let a human retype the tags, and now that retyping correctly changes which matcher applies.

decisions.question: What did refusing every named matcher cost, and what does it teach about testing?
decisions.commitment: It broke the only client. Test the client, not only the endpoint.
decisions.why: The refusal was right in principle and shipped as a regression, because the only client sends the field unconditionally: the Match view's picker is a <select> that always has a value, so every click on a custom-matcher surface got a 400 blaming the caller for a field the page filled in itself. The test written for the refusal passed precisely because it posted the field explicitly — it certified the regression instead of catching it. Two changes, and the second is the general lesson: accept a name that agrees with what is in force (a caller asking for what is already true is not asking for something else), and test the client, not only the endpoint. An API-layer test cannot catch a client sending the wrong thing, which is exactly how this shipped.

decisions.question: How far does the matcher have to be threaded before the fix is real?
decisions.commitment: Past tier 1. Engine.translate takes a matcher, or the same response uses two.
decisions.why: The threading stopped where §6.40's measurement stopped — at the sealed-memory lookup — and the audit found tier 2 still keying with the process-wide matcher. In a custom domain the query's norm and each row's stored norm are then unrelated key spaces, so the offline engine matched nothing: every unsealed query landed `pending` and never entered the review queue, and the Claude engine got no verified-TM context. Silently, in both cases; a reviewer just sees an empty queue and concludes the machine had no opinion. The generalisable part is that an entry's measured table is a floor and not a map — §6.40 measured the seal and rejection paths because those are where the human acts, and the fix had to cover every path that keys anything, which is a strictly larger set. Widened in the same shape as `store=` and tolerated the same way, so a custom engine on the old signature keeps working.
